lead: A one-way slab bends in one direction only, across its short span. It happens when the slab rests on two opposite edges, or on four edges with the long span l<sub>y</sub> more than twice the short span l<sub>x</sub>. The design takes a strip 1 m wide across the short span and designs it as a beam 1000 mm wide. Floors of corridors, verandahs and long narrow rooms are one-way slabs.
prereq: You need the limit state design of singly reinforced beams (the stress block, x<sub>u,max</sub>, the A<sub>st</sub> formula) and the IS 456 shear strength τ<sub>c</sub>.

blocks.text: Think of a slab on four edges as two sets of crossing strips that must deflect the same amount where they cross. A simply supported strip deflects in proportion to l⁴, so the shorter strip is much stiffer and takes most of the load. With l<sub>y</sub> = 2l<sub>x</sub> the short strip is 2⁴ = 16 times stiffer and carries 16/17 ≈ 94 % of the load.

IS 456 therefore designs a slab with ly/lx > 2 as one-way: only the short-span strips are designed for bending, and the long direction gets the minimum steel. A slab on two opposite supports is one-way whatever the ratio. When ly/lx ≤ 2 the slab is two-way; see Two-way slabs with various edge conditions.

A load of w kN/m² on the slab is a line load of w kN/m on a 1 m strip, the same number. Then b = 1000 mm and the beam depth is the slab thickness D. The effective depth is d = D − nominal cover − φ/2, where φ is the main bar diameter.

sections.h3: The IS 456 rules a slab design uses

items: Effective span (cl. 22.2): the smaller of clear span + d and the centre-to-centre distance of the supports.

Deflection (cl. 23.2): span/effective depth must not exceed the basic value (20 simply supported, 26 continuous, 7 cantilever) times the Fig. 4 modification factor. The factor depends on the steel percentage p<sub>t</sub> and the service stress f<sub>s</sub> = 0.58 f<sub>y</sub> × (A<sub>st</sub> required/A<sub>st</sub> provided); near p<sub>t</sub> = 0.3 % it is about 1.5, so start with l/d ≈ 28.
Minimum steel (cl. 26.5.2.1): 0.12 % of bD for Fe415 bars, 0.15 % for mild steel, for main and distribution steel. Bar diameter at most D/8.
Maximum spacing (cl. 26.3.3): main bars the smaller of 3d and 300 mm; distribution bars the smaller of 5d and 450 mm.
Nominal cover (Table 16): 20 mm for mild exposure (15 mm allowed for bars of 12 mm or less), 30 mm for moderate.
Shear (cl. 40.2.1.1): no stirrups are needed if τ<sub>v</sub> ≤ kτ<sub>c</sub>, with τ<sub>c</sub> from Table 19 and the depth factor k = 1.30 for D ≤ 150 mm, falling to 1.00 at 300 mm.

blocks.text: M<sub>u</sub> = w<sub>u</sub> l² / 8,   V<sub>u</sub> = w<sub>u</sub> l / 2
blocks.where: w<sub>u</sub> is the factored load, 1.5 × (dead + live), in kN/m on the strip; l is the effective span in m.

blocks.text: A<sub>st</sub> = (0.5 f<sub>ck</sub> / f<sub>y</sub>) [1 − √(1 − 4.6 M<sub>u</sub> /(f<sub>ck</sub> b d²))] b d
blocks.where: This is the Annex G equation M<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> d (1 − A<sub>st</sub> f<sub>y</sub>/(b d f<sub>ck</sub>)) solved for A<sub>st</sub>, valid while M<sub>u</sub> ≤ M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 f<sub>ck</sub> b d² (Fe415). The flexure tables of SP 16 give the same p<sub>t</sub> from M<sub>u</sub>/bd².

blocks.text: Distribution steel runs along the long span, on top of the main bars, which stay in the outer layer to keep the larger d. It holds the main bars during concreting, controls shrinkage and temperature cracks, and spreads a point load to several main bars. If the deflection check fails, increase D and repeat the design.

examples.question: Design a simply supported one-way slab for a room 3.0 m × 7.5 m (clear) with 230 mm walls on all sides. Live load 3 kN/m², floor finish 1 kN/m², M20, Fe415, mild exposure (20 mm cover, 10 mm bars).
steps: Type: l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub> = 7.5/3.0 = 2.5 > 2, so the slab spans one way, across 3.0 m.
Effective span: 3.0 + 0.115 = 3.115 m, or centre to centre 3.230 m. Take l = 3.115 m.
Loads: self weight 0.140 × 25 = 3.50, finish 1.00, live 3.00; w = 7.50 kN/m², w<sub>u</sub> = 1.5 × 7.50 = 11.250 kN/m².
M<sub>u</sub> = 11.250 × 3.115²/8 = 13.65 kN·m/m; V<sub>u</sub> = 11.250 × 3.115/2 = 17.52 kN/m. M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 × 20 × 1000 × 115² = 36.50 kN·m, larger, so under-reinforced.
10 mm bars (78.54 mm²): 1000 × 78.54/351 = 224 mm. Provide 10 mm @ 220 mm c/c = 357 mm²/m (220 < 3d and 300 mm).
Distribution: 168 mm²/m with 8 mm bars: 1000 × 50.27/168 = 299 mm. Provide 8 mm @ 290 mm c/c (173 mm²/m).

Deflection: f<sub>s</sub> = 0.58 × 415 × 351/357 = 237 N/mm²; with p<sub>t</sub> = 0.31 % the factor is about 1.49. Allowed l/d = 20 × 1.49 = 29.8; actual 3115/115 = 27.1. Safe. (A 130 mm slab, d = 105 mm, fails: l/d = 29.6 against about 27.8.)
examples.answer: D = 140 mm; main steel 10 mm @ 220 mm c/c (357 mm²/m) across the 3.0 m span at the bottom; distribution steel 8 mm @ 290 mm c/c along the long span. M<sub>u</sub> = 13.65 kN·m/m; shear and deflection pass.

traps: Using the clear span or the wall centre lines without comparing: the effective span is the smaller of the two rules, here 3.115 m, not 3.0 m (unsafe) or 3.23 m.
Writing the strip load in kN: 11.25 kN/m² on a 1 m strip is 11.25 kN/m, and b = 1000 mm, not the room width.
Checking deflection with the basic ratio 20 alone, or with the steel first assumed. The limit is 20 × the factor for the steel actually provided, here 20 × 1.49 = 29.8.
Spacing distribution bars at 3d or placing them below the main bars. Their limit is the smaller of 5d and 450 mm, and they go on top.

quiz.q: When does IS 456 treat a slab supported on four edges as one-way?
quiz.a: When l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub> > 2; it is then designed as strips spanning the short way.

quiz.q: State the minimum steel and maximum main-bar spacing for an Fe415 slab 150 mm thick with d = 125 mm.
quiz.a: Minimum 0.12 % × 1000 × 150 = 180 mm²/m; spacing the smaller of 3 × 125 = 375 mm and 300 mm, so 300 mm.

quiz.q: Why does the short span carry most of the load when l<sub>y</sub> = 2l<sub>x</sub>?
quiz.a: Crossing strips deflect equally and deflection varies as l⁴, so the short strip is 16 times stiffer and takes 16/17 ≈ 94 % of the load.

quiz.q: A one-way strip has w<sub>u</sub> = 12 kN/m², l = 3.5 m and d = 110 mm (M20, Fe415). Find M<sub>u</sub> and A<sub>st</sub>.
A 130 mm slab has 10 mm bars @ 200 mm (d = 105 mm), M20, Fe415, effective span 2.8 m, finish 1 kN/m². Find the safe live load.
quiz.a: A<sub>st</sub> = 392.7 mm²/m, x<sub>u</sub> = 19.7 mm, M<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 × 415 × 392.7 × (105 − 0.42 × 19.7) = 13.71 kN·m/m. w<sub>u</sub> = 8 × 13.71/2.8² = 13.99 kN/m², w = 9.33 kN/m², dead load 4.25, so live load ≈ 5.1 kN/m². Deflection: l/d = 26.7 against about 27.2, passes.

quiz.q: A student takes l = 3.0 m (clear span) for the slab of the worked example. Is the design safe?
quiz.a: No. M<sub>u</sub> becomes 11.25 × 3.0²/8 = 12.66 kN·m/m instead of 13.65, about 7 % low, so the steel is under-designed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real slabs are analysed with finite element plate models that show the load sharing directly, and long one-way floors are often made as ribbed slabs or precast hollow-core planks to save weight. Long-term deflection also depends on creep, shrinkage and construction order, which the span/depth rule covers only roughly. Search for "ribbed slab design" and "long-term deflection of slabs".

figure.caption: The 3.0 m × 7.5 m room spans one way, across 3.0 m. A 1 m strip carries 11.25 kN/m over 3.115 m, so the moment at mid-span is 13.65 kN·m per metre; the main bars sit at the bottom with the distribution bars on top of them.
